notes.front: What is formal communication in ICS?
notes.back: Communication that follows the chain of command: required for work assignments, resource requests and progress reports.
notes.explanation: Keeping taskings on a formal line means every assignment can be traced back to an authorised supervisor.
notes.example: Like a work order routed through your supervisor, never a rumour passed down the hallway.
notes.source: IS-0200.c Student Manual (September 2020), Lesson 2, Visual 9, SM-41

notes.front: What is informal communication in ICS, and what must it never be used for?
notes.back: Information passed horizontally or vertically without restriction; never for resource requests or work assignments.
notes.explanation: It keeps everyone abreast of the situation, but taskings still have to travel the formal line.
notes.example: Like two colleagues comparing notes by the coffee machine: useful, but not how you get a work order.
notes.source: IS-0200.c Student Manual (September 2020), Lesson 2, Visuals 10-11, SM-42/SM-43

notes.front: In ICS, what is a Director?
notes.back: The ICS title for the person supervising a branch; also the title for the person managing a team in an EOC.
notes.explanation: A Director sits between a Section Chief and the smaller elements that a branch contains.
notes.example: Like a regional head who reports to a national Chief and has local managers reporting up to them.
notes.source: National Incident Management System, Third Edition (October 2017), Glossary, p. 73

notes.front: In ICS, what is a Supervisor?
notes.back: The ICS title for the person responsible for one of the smaller operational subdivisions below a branch.
notes.explanation: Supervisor sits a level below Director on the ICS title ladder; the next lesson names what those subdivisions are.
notes.example: Like a shift supervisor who reports up to a branch manager.
notes.source: National Incident Management System, Third Edition (October 2017), Glossary, p. 80

notes.front: In ICS, what is a Leader?
notes.back: The ICS title for the person supervising a unit, strike team, resource team or task force.
notes.explanation: Leader covers supervision from a full unit down to a single strike team, resource team or task force.
notes.example: Like the lead of a small crew sent out together on one task.
notes.source: National Incident Management System, Third Edition (October 2017), Glossary, p. 76

notes.front: In ICS, what is a Manager?
notes.back: The individual within an ICS unit assigned specific managerial responsibilities, such as a Staging Area Manager or Camp Manager.
notes.explanation: Manager is a support title used for a defined slice of a unit's workload, not a supervisory level of its own.
notes.example: Like a named lead for one site (a staging area or camp) rather than for a whole unit.
notes.source: National Incident Management System, Third Edition (October 2017), Glossary, p. 76

notes.front: What is a Single Resource in ICS?
notes.back: An individual, a piece of equipment with its crew, or a team with an identified work supervisor, usable on an incident.
notes.explanation: It is the smallest building block ICS assigns work to directly.
notes.example: Like one fire engine and its crew, reporting to one named supervisor.
notes.source: National Incident Management System, Third Edition (October 2017), Glossary, p. 80

notes.front: What is an After-Action Review (AAR)?
notes.back: An assessment method carried out after a major activity to find out what happened and why.
notes.explanation: It is one of several ways ICS organisations capture lessons once the response, or a major phase of it, is over.
notes.example: Like a post-match review: what happened, and what would the team do differently?
notes.source: IS-0200.c Student Manual (September 2020), Lesson 2, Visual 22, SM-56

notes.front: What three features define Unified Command?
notes.back: Common objectives and strategies; joint decisions from a single command structure at one shared post; it still maintains unity of command.
notes.explanation: Agencies decide together, but each employee still reports to only one supervisor.
notes.source: IS-0200.c Student Manual (September 2020), Lesson 2, Visual 5, SM-36

notes.front: Which advantage of Unified Command is about having one shared set of objectives?
notes.back: A single set of objectives guides the response.
notes.explanation: Unified Command lets several agencies with jurisdiction manage one incident together instead of separately.
notes.source: IS-0200.c Student Manual (September 2020), Lesson 2, Visual 6, SM-37

notes.front: Which advantage of Unified Command is about strategy being developed collectively?
notes.back: A collective approach develops the strategy for the incident.
notes.explanation: Unified Command lets several agencies with jurisdiction manage one incident together instead of separately.
notes.source: IS-0200.c Student Manual (September 2020), Lesson 2, Visual 6, SM-37

notes.front: Which advantage of Unified Command is about information flowing better between everyone involved?
notes.back: Information flow and coordination improve between everyone involved.
notes.explanation: Unified Command lets several agencies with jurisdiction manage one incident together instead of separately.
notes.source: IS-0200.c Student Manual (September 2020), Lesson 2, Visual 6, SM-37

notes.front: Which advantage of Unified Command is about all agencies understanding shared priorities and restrictions?
notes.back: All agencies understand the joint priorities and restrictions.
notes.explanation: Unified Command lets several agencies with jurisdiction manage one incident together instead of separately.
notes.source: IS-0200.c Student Manual (September 2020), Lesson 2, Visual 6, SM-37

notes.front: Which advantage of Unified Command is about agencies keeping their own legal authority?
notes.back: No agency's legal authority is compromised or neglected.
notes.explanation: Unified Command lets several agencies with jurisdiction manage one incident together instead of separately.
notes.source: IS-0200.c Student Manual (September 2020), Lesson 2, Visual 6, SM-37

notes.front: Which advantage of Unified Command is about working from one shared Incident Action Plan?
notes.back: Agencies optimise their efforts under a single Incident Action Plan.
notes.explanation: Unified Command lets several agencies with jurisdiction manage one incident together instead of separately.
notes.source: IS-0200.c Student Manual (September 2020), Lesson 2, Visual 6, SM-37

notes.front: Which leadership responsibility is about giving specific instructions and asking for feedback?
notes.back: Communicates by giving specific instructions and asking for feedback.
notes.explanation: These are the everyday behaviours the manual expects of anyone leading responders, not just of the Incident Commander.
notes.source: IS-0200.c Student Manual (September 2020), Lesson 2, Visual 14, SM-47

notes.front: Which leadership responsibility is about supervising the scene of action?
notes.back: Supervises the scene of action.
notes.explanation: These are the everyday behaviours the manual expects of anyone leading responders, not just of the Incident Commander.
notes.source: IS-0200.c Student Manual (September 2020), Lesson 2, Visual 14, SM-47

notes.front: Which leadership responsibility is about checking whether the plan is working?
notes.back: Evaluates the effectiveness of the plan.
notes.explanation: These are the everyday behaviours the manual expects of anyone leading responders, not just of the Incident Commander.
notes.source: IS-0200.c Student Manual (September 2020), Lesson 2, Visual 14, SM-47

notes.front: Which leadership responsibility is about being ready to change plans or instructions?
notes.back: Understands and accepts the need to modify plans or instructions.
notes.explanation: These are the everyday behaviours the manual expects of anyone leading responders, not just of the Incident Commander.
notes.source: IS-0200.c Student Manual (September 2020), Lesson 2, Visual 14, SM-47

notes.front: Which leadership responsibility is about ensuring safe work practices?
notes.back: Ensures safe work practices.
notes.explanation: These are the everyday behaviours the manual expects of anyone leading responders, not just of the Incident Commander.
notes.source: IS-0200.c Student Manual (September 2020), Lesson 2, Visual 14, SM-47

notes.front: Which leadership responsibility is about taking command of assigned resources?
notes.back: Takes command of assigned resources.
notes.explanation: These are the everyday behaviours the manual expects of anyone leading responders, not just of the Incident Commander.
notes.source: IS-0200.c Student Manual (September 2020), Lesson 2, Visual 14, SM-47

notes.front: Which leadership responsibility is about motivating with a “can do safely” attitude?
notes.back: Motivates with a “can do safely” attitude.
notes.explanation: These are the everyday behaviours the manual expects of anyone leading responders, not just of the Incident Commander.
notes.source: IS-0200.c Student Manual (September 2020), Lesson 2, Visual 14, SM-47

notes.front: Which leadership responsibility is about taking action rather than waiting to be told?
notes.back: Demonstrates initiative by taking action.
notes.explanation: These are the everyday behaviours the manual expects of anyone leading responders, not just of the Incident Commander.
notes.source: IS-0200.c Student Manual (September 2020), Lesson 2, Visual 14, SM-47

notes.front: Among the common leadership responsibilities, which one is the first duty of ICS leadership?
notes.back: The safety of all personnel; ensuring safe work practices is the top priority.
notes.explanation: Everything else a leader does sits underneath this duty, from Team Leader up to Unified Command.
notes.source: IS-0200.c Student Manual (September 2020), Lesson 2, Visual 14 note, SM-47

notes.front: What three values must a leader demonstrate to be effective, according to the manual?
notes.back: Commitment to duty, respect, and integrity.
notes.explanation: These values sit behind the specific leadership responsibilities: they are what makes carrying them out credible.
notes.source: IS-0200.c Student Manual (September 2020), Lesson 2, Visual 15, SM-48

notes.front: A complete briefing states clear objectives and three other elements. What are they?
notes.back: Task (what is to be done), purpose (why), and end state (how it should look when done).
notes.explanation: Stating the purpose and end state, not just the task, lets a team adapt if the situation changes.
notes.source: IS-0200.c Instructor Guide (September 2020), Lesson 2, Visual 21, IG-79

notes.front: What four incident management assessment methods does the manual list?
notes.back: Corrective action report/After-Action Review (AAR), debriefing, post-incident critique, and mitigation plans.
notes.explanation: Assessment happens after a major activity so leaders and responders can find out what happened and why.
notes.source: IS-0200.c Student Manual (September 2020), Lesson 2, Visual 22, SM-56

notes.front: What happens to the ICS organisation when a supervisor's span of control is exceeded?
notes.back: Additional Teams, Divisions, Groups, Branches or Sections are added; when a supervisor has too few, elements are reorganised or demobilised.
notes.explanation: ICS follows a “form follows function” philosophy: the organisation's size is set through incident planning, not fixed in advance.
notes.source: IS-0200.c Student Manual (September 2020), Lesson 2, Visual 29, SM-66

notes.front: Which reason for standard ICS position titles is about a shared understanding across agencies?
notes.back: It provides a common standard understood across agencies.
notes.explanation: A title such as “Division Supervisor” means the same thing to every responder, whatever their home agency.
notes.source: IS-0200.c Student Manual (September 2020), Lesson 2, Visual 32, SM-69

notes.front: Which reason for standard ICS position titles is about making sure the role is filled by someone qualified?
notes.back: It ensures qualified individuals fill the positions.
notes.explanation: A title such as “Division Supervisor” means the same thing to every responder, whatever their home agency.
notes.source: IS-0200.c Student Manual (September 2020), Lesson 2, Visual 32, SM-69

notes.front: Which reason for standard ICS position titles is about confirming that requested personnel are actually qualified?
notes.back: It ensures that requested personnel are, in fact, qualified.
notes.explanation: A title such as “Division Supervisor” means the same thing to every responder, whatever their home agency.
notes.source: IS-0200.c Student Manual (September 2020), Lesson 2, Visual 32, SM-69

notes.front: Which reason for standard ICS position titles is about standardising communication about who does what?
notes.back: It standardises communication about who does what.
notes.explanation: A title such as “Division Supervisor” means the same thing to every responder, whatever their home agency.
notes.source: IS-0200.c Student Manual (September 2020), Lesson 2, Visual 32, SM-69

notes.front: Which reason for standard ICS position titles is about the title itself describing the role’s responsibilities?
notes.back: It describes the responsibilities that come with the position.
notes.explanation: A title such as “Division Supervisor” means the same thing to every responder, whatever their home agency.
notes.source: IS-0200.c Student Manual (September 2020), Lesson 2, Visual 32, SM-69

notes.front: In the ICS supervisory title ladder, what title is used for the person leading Incident Command?
notes.back: Incident Commander
notes.explanation: Titles for all ICS supervisory levels are standard: the next lesson names what each organisational level actually does.
notes.source: IS-0200.c Student Manual (September 2020), Lesson 2, Visual 33, SM-70

notes.front: In the ICS supervisory title ladder, what title is used for the person leading Command Staff?
notes.back: Officer
notes.explanation: Titles for all ICS supervisory levels are standard: the next lesson names what each organisational level actually does.
notes.source: IS-0200.c Student Manual (September 2020), Lesson 2, Visual 33, SM-70

notes.front: In the ICS supervisory title ladder, what title is used for the person leading a Section?
notes.back: Chief
notes.explanation: Titles for all ICS supervisory levels are standard: the next lesson names what each organisational level actually does.
notes.source: IS-0200.c Student Manual (September 2020), Lesson 2, Visual 33, SM-70

notes.front: In the ICS supervisory title ladder, what title is used for the person leading a branch?
notes.back: Director
notes.explanation: Titles for all ICS supervisory levels are standard: the next lesson names what each organisational level actually does.
notes.source: IS-0200.c Student Manual (September 2020), Lesson 2, Visual 33, SM-70

notes.front: In the ICS supervisory title ladder, what title is used for the person leading a smaller geographic or functional subdivision within a branch?
notes.back: Supervisor
notes.explanation: Titles for all ICS supervisory levels are standard: the next lesson names what each organisational level actually does.
notes.source: IS-0200.c Student Manual (September 2020), Lesson 2, Visual 33, SM-70

notes.front: In the ICS supervisory title ladder, what title is used for the person leading a unit?
notes.back: Unit Leader
notes.explanation: Titles for all ICS supervisory levels are standard: the next lesson names what each organisational level actually does.
notes.source: IS-0200.c Student Manual (September 2020), Lesson 2, Visual 33, SM-70

notes.front: In the ICS supervisory title ladder, what title is used for the person leading a matched team or task-oriented group of resources?
notes.back: Leader
notes.explanation: Titles for all ICS supervisory levels are standard: the next lesson names what each organisational level actually does.
notes.source: IS-0200.c Student Manual (September 2020), Lesson 2, Visual 33, SM-70

notes.front: What is the support-position title for Incident Command, a Section, or a branch?
notes.back: Deputy
notes.explanation: Support titles name the helper position at each level; only a Deputy can take over.
notes.source: IS-0200.c Student Manual (September 2020), Lesson 2, Visual 33, SM-70

notes.front: What is the support-position title for Command Staff?
notes.back: Assistant
notes.explanation: Support titles name the helper position at each level; only a Deputy can take over.
notes.source: IS-0200.c Student Manual (September 2020), Lesson 2, Visual 33, SM-70

notes.front: What is the support-position title for a unit?
notes.back: Manager
notes.explanation: Support titles name the helper position at each level; only a Deputy can take over.
notes.source: IS-0200.c Student Manual (September 2020), Lesson 2, Visual 33, SM-70

notes.front: What is the support-position title for a smaller geographic or functional subdivision within a branch?
notes.back: no support title (N/A)
notes.explanation: Support titles name the helper position at each level; only a Deputy can take over.
notes.source: IS-0200.c Student Manual (September 2020), Lesson 2, Visual 33, SM-70

notes.front: Roughly what share of incidents are small responses handled by Command and single resources alone?
notes.back: Approximately 95%.
notes.explanation: Most incidents never need Divisions, Groups or Branches; the ICS organisation only grows when the incident does.
notes.source: IS-0200.c Student Manual (September 2020), Lesson 2, Visual 30, SM-67

notes.front: Which shared communication responsibility is about briefing other people as needed?
notes.back: Brief others as needed.
notes.explanation: These responsibilities keep critical information flowing; face-to-face is the most effective way to carry them out.
notes.source: IS-0200.c Student Manual (September 2020), Lesson 2, Visual 20, SM-54

notes.front: Which shared communication responsibility is about debriefing your own actions?
notes.back: Debrief their own actions.
notes.explanation: These responsibilities keep critical information flowing; face-to-face is the most effective way to carry them out.
notes.source: IS-0200.c Student Manual (September 2020), Lesson 2, Visual 20, SM-54

notes.front: Which shared communication responsibility is about warning others of hazards?
notes.back: Communicate hazards to others.
notes.explanation: These responsibilities keep critical information flowing; face-to-face is the most effective way to carry them out.
notes.source: IS-0200.c Student Manual (September 2020), Lesson 2, Visual 20, SM-54

notes.front: Which shared communication responsibility is about acknowledging messages you receive?
notes.back: Acknowledge messages.
notes.explanation: These responsibilities keep critical information flowing; face-to-face is the most effective way to carry them out.
notes.source: IS-0200.c Student Manual (September 2020), Lesson 2, Visual 20, SM-54

notes.front: Which shared communication responsibility is about asking when you do not know something?
notes.back: Ask if they do not know.
notes.explanation: These responsibilities keep critical information flowing; face-to-face is the most effective way to carry them out.
notes.source: IS-0200.c Student Manual (September 2020), Lesson 2, Visual 20, SM-54

notes.front: Three agencies with jurisdiction over a wildfire set joint objectives and run the incident from one shared command post, each keeping its own legal authority. What ICS feature is this?
notes.back: Unified Command.
notes.choices:
A) Unified Command
B) A mutual aid agreement
C) Two separate Incident Commanders, each running their own command post
notes.choicesExplained: B: mutual aid only shares resources, it does not merge command. C: that is two separate commands, not one shared Unified Command.
notes.explanation: Joint objectives, one command structure at one post, with unity of command preserved, are Unified Command's defining features.
notes.source: IS-0200.c Student Manual (September 2020), Lesson 2, Visual 5, SM-36

notes.front: A responder asks why their agency should give up running its own command post and join a Unified Command instead. What is the best answer?
notes.back: A single set of objectives and one Incident Action Plan improve coordination, without any agency losing its legal authority.
notes.explanation: Unified Command is not a loss of authority; it is a shared decision structure that keeps each agency's authority intact.
notes.source: IS-0200.c Student Manual (September 2020), Lesson 2, Visual 6, SM-37

notes.front: A Division Supervisor radios the Operations Section Chief to request two more engines. Is that formal or informal communication?
notes.back: Formal communication: it is a request for additional resources, so it must follow the chain of command.
notes.explanation: Formal communication is required whenever work is assigned, resources are requested, or progress is reported.
notes.source: IS-0200.c Student Manual (September 2020), Lesson 2, Visual 9, SM-41

notes.front: The Supply Unit Leader mentions a shortage of tents directly to the Logistics Section Chief, outside the chain of command. Is that allowed?
notes.back: Yes: that is informal communication, used to exchange incident information, but it could never be used to task work or request resources.
notes.explanation: Informal communication lets information flow freely; it just cannot substitute for a formal assignment or request.
notes.source: IS-0200.c Student Manual (September 2020), Lesson 2, Visual 11, SM-43

notes.front: A Division Supervisor must choose between finishing a task on schedule and stopping work because conditions have become unsafe. What does ICS leadership doctrine say comes first?
notes.back: Safety.
notes.choices:
A) Finish the task, then address safety
B) Stop unsafe work; safety is the top priority
C) Ask the Incident Commander before doing either
notes.choicesExplained: A: this reverses the stated priority. C: ensuring safe work practices is already named as the top priority, so no separate permission step is described.
notes.explanation: Ensuring safe work practices is named as the top priority among all the common leadership responsibilities.
notes.source: IS-0200.c Student Manual (September 2020), Lesson 2, Visual 14 note, SM-47

notes.front: An Operations Section Chief now has twelve single resources reporting directly, well past any workable span of control. What should happen to the organisation?
notes.back: It should expand: resources are organised into Teams, Divisions, Groups, Branches or Sections to bring the span of control back to a workable ratio.
notes.choices:
A) Leave the structure as it is
B) Add organisational layers to restore span of control
C) Reduce the number of resources on scene
notes.choicesExplained: A: an unmanageable span of control is unsafe and inefficient. C: the incident's needs, not the org chart, determine how many resources are required.
notes.explanation: ICS follows “form follows function”: the size of the organisation grows and shrinks with the incident, not the other way round.
notes.source: IS-0200.c Student Manual (September 2020), Lesson 2, Visual 29, SM-66

notes.front: A mutual aid crew arrives and is told to report to the “Division A Supervisor.” Why does that title matter more than the crew's own agency rank?
notes.back: Standard ICS titles work the same way for every agency, so the crew immediately knows who to report to and what that person's role is.
notes.explanation: Position titles describe the responsibility of the position, not the rank of whoever fills it.
notes.source: IS-0200.c Student Manual (September 2020), Lesson 2, Visual 32, SM-69

notes.front: You are told to report to “the Chief.” At what ICS organisational level does that title apply?
notes.back: Section: Chief is the title for the person leading one of the ICS Sections (Operations, Planning, Logistics, Finance/Administration).
notes.explanation: Each ICS organisational level has its own standard supervisory title.
notes.source: IS-0200.c Student Manual (September 2020), Lesson 2, Visual 33, SM-70

notes.front: A branch grows large enough that its Director needs a stand-in able to take over part of the workload. What is that support position called?
notes.back: Deputy.
notes.choices:
A) Deputy
B) Assistant
C) Manager
notes.choicesExplained: B: Assistant is the support title for Command Staff, not for a branch. C: Manager supports a unit, not a branch.
notes.explanation: Support titles are level-specific: Deputy supports Incident Command, Sections and branches; Assistant supports Command Staff; Manager supports units; Single Resource Boss supports a Strike Team/Task Force.
notes.source: IS-0200.c Student Manual (September 2020), Lesson 2, Visual 33, SM-70

notes.front: Someone introduces themselves as the “Logistics Service Branch Director.” What ICS level are they leading?
notes.back: A branch.
notes.explanation: Director is the standard ICS title for the person leading a branch.
notes.source: National Incident Management System, Third Edition (October 2017), Glossary, p. 73

notes.front: Someone is introduced as a “Supervisor.” What can you conclude about the level they lead, without knowing anything else?
notes.back: They lead one of the smaller geographic or functional subdivisions inside a branch, one level below a Director.
notes.explanation: ICS titles reveal a person's level in the organisation before you know anything else about the incident.
notes.source: National Incident Management System, Third Edition (October 2017), Glossary, p. 80

notes.front: A group of five identical fire engines, working together under one supervisor, needs its supervisor titled. What is the correct ICS title?
notes.back: Leader.
notes.explanation: Leader is used for the person supervising a matched team or unit of resources.
notes.source: National Incident Management System, Third Edition (October 2017), Glossary, p. 76

notes.front: One ambulance and its two-person crew, reporting to a named supervisor, arrives at an incident. How is this classified in ICS?
notes.back: A Single Resource.
notes.explanation: A Single Resource is the smallest unit ICS assigns work to directly: one piece of equipment (or person) with an identified supervisor.
notes.source: National Incident Management System, Third Edition (October 2017), Glossary, p. 80

notes.front: What is the difference between unity of command and Unified Command?
notes.back: Unity of command: each person reports to one supervisor. Unified Command: several agencies jointly command one incident with shared objectives.
notes.explanation: Unified Command does not break unity of command: within it, each responder still has exactly one supervisor.
notes.contrast: One is a reporting rule for individuals; the other is a command structure for agencies.
notes.source: IS-0200.c Student Manual (September 2020), Lesson 2, Visual 3, SM-34

notes.front: What is the difference between formal and informal communication in ICS?
notes.back: Formal: follows the chain of command; required for assignments, resource requests and progress reports. Informal: information only, passed freely, never for tasking.
notes.explanation: Both keep the organisation informed, but only formal communication can create or change a work assignment.
notes.contrast: Formal communication commits someone to an action; informal communication only shares information.
notes.source: IS-0200.c Student Manual (September 2020), Lesson 2, Visuals 9-11, SM-41/SM-43

notes.front: Officer, Chief, Director, Supervisor and Leader all sound like general management titles. What actually distinguishes them in ICS?
notes.back: Each names one fixed organisational level, from Command Staff (Officer) down to a unit or team (Leader).
notes.explanation: The titles are not ranks or job grades; a person's ICS title is set entirely by which level of the organisation they lead.
notes.contrast: Outside ICS these words suggest seniority; inside ICS they only say which organisational level someone leads.
notes.source: IS-0200.c Student Manual (September 2020), Lesson 2, Visual 33, SM-70

notes.front: What is the support-position title for a Strike Team or Task Force?
notes.back: Single Resource Boss
notes.explanation: Support titles name the helper position at each level; only a Deputy can take over.
notes.source: IS-0200.c Student Manual (September 2020), Lesson 2, Visual 33, SM-70
